models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The main reason is conflicts of interest: a firm that declines to represent the big money-center banks stays free to sue them.

Under professional conduct rules, a firm generally cannot act against a current client, and prior work for a former client can also bar related matters. The largest banks are involved in an enormous share of major commercial disputes, as lenders, underwriters, trustees, counterparties and advisers. A firm that takes even small assignments from them can find itself locked out of lucrative cases against them. Banks have sometimes been accused of spreading work around widely for exactly this effect.

Staying "conflict-free" therefore becomes a strategic position. The firm can take large plaintiff-side or adverse cases, such as mortgage-backed securities claims, rate-rigging and antitrust actions, or bankruptcy and creditor disputes. These are often on contingency or alternative fees with very large upside. It also becomes the go-to choice for hedge funds, insurers, investors and companies that need counsel most established firms cannot provide.

Quinn Emanuel is the best-known example: it has openly marketed its policy of not representing the major money-center banks so it can litigate against them. This is from memory; I did not run a search.

Large banks reinforce this barrier through strict outside counsel guidelines that prohibit panel firms from suing the bank or any of its sprawling affiliates, while using their massive legal budgets to withhold business from firms that take adverse positions. The economics reinforce this strategy. Large banks exert heavy fee pressure, impose strict billing guidelines, and demand steep discounts from panel counsel. Representing adversaries against them, by contrast, allows a firm to command premium rates or lucrative contingency and hybrid fee arrangements without getting conflicted out of the market's biggest cases.
